title: Quick Sort
definition: Quick Sort is a highly efficient comparison sort based on the divide-and-conquer paradigm. It works by selecting a 'pivot' element from the array and partitioning the other elements into two sub-arrays, according to whether they are less than or greater than the pivot. The sub-arrays are then sorted recursively. Quick Sort is usually faster than other O(n log n) algorithms like merge sort and heap sort.
conceptExplanation: Quick Sort follows divide-and-conquer: 1) Choose a pivot element. 2) Partition the array so elements < pivot are on left and elements > pivot are on right. 3) Recursively sort the sub-arrays. The choice of pivot and partitioning strategy greatly affects performance. Average case O(n log n), worst case O(n²) (when pivot is smallest/largest element consistently).
keyPoints: - Divide and conquer - Pivot selection - Partitioning - Recursive sorting - Average O(n log n), worst O(n²)
importantTerminology: Quick Sort, Pivot, Partition, Divide and Conquer, In-place
workingPrinciple: The algorithm selects a pivot (commonly first, last, middle, or random element). It then partitions the array: all elements less than pivot go to left, greater go to right. The pivot is now in its final sorted position. This process recurses on the left and right sub-arrays. Partitioning can be done using Lomuto scheme (simple, uses last element as pivot) or Hoare scheme (more efficient, uses first element as pivot).
realLifeExample: Sorting large datasets, database sorting, efficient general-purpose sort
dsaExample: Sorting array [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70] with pivot 30: partition → [10], [30], [40, 50, 70, 90, 80], then recursively sort sub-arrays
diagram: Quick sort partition: [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70] choosing pivot=70 (last element), partition: [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50] | [70] | [] elements < 70 on left, greater on right
algorithm:
Quick Sort Algorithm (Lomuto Partition Scheme):
1. QUICKSORT(arr, low, high)
2. IF low < high
3.   SET pi = PARTITION(arr, low, high)
4.   QUICKSORT(arr, low, pi - 1)
5.   QUICKSORT(arr, pi + 1, high)
6. END IF

PARTITION(arr, low, high):
1. SET pivot = arr[high]
2. SET i = low - 1
3. FOR j = low TO high - 1
4.   IF arr[j] < pivot
5.     SET i = i + 1
5.     SWAP arr[i], arr[j]
6.   END IF
7. END FOR
6. SWAP arr[i + 1], arr[high]
7. RETURN i + 1

HOARE Partition Scheme alternative: first element as pivot, two-pointer approach.
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  FUNCTION quicksort(arr, low, high)
    IF low < high
      SET pi = partition(arr, low, high)
      quicksort(arr, low, pi - 1)
      quicksort(arr, pi + 1, high)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION

  FUNCTION partition(arr, low, high)
    SET pivot = arr[high]
    SET i = low - 1
    FOR j = low TO high - 1
      IF arr[j] < pivot
        SET i = i + 1
        SWAP arr[i] WITH arr[j]
      END IF
    END FOR
    SWAP arr[i + 1] WITH arr[high]
    RETURN i + 1
  END FUNCTION
END
complexity:
Time: Best case O(n log n) - balanced partitions
Average case O(n log n)
Worst case O(n²) - smallest or largest pivot consistently (e.g., already sorted with first/pivot choice)
Space: O(log n) - recursive call stack

Optimizations: Random pivot, median-of-three pivot, tail recursion elimination
applications: General-purpose sorting, large datasets, when average-case performance is critical
advantages: Average O(n log n) performance, in-place O(log n) space, cache-friendly, typically faster than merge/heap sort in practice
limitations: Worst case O(n²) if pivot selection is poor, not stable, performance varies with input and pivot choice
commonMistakes: Poor pivot choice (always first/last on sorted data), not handling duplicate elements well, stack overflow with deep recursion, incorrect partition logic
importantExamPoints:
Pivot selection strategies: first, last, middle, random, median-of-three
Lomuto vs Hoare partition scheme
Worst case avoidance: random pivot or median-of-three
Best case: O(n log n) with balanced partitions
Average case: O(n log n) regardless of input (with good pivot)
Not stable - equal elements may change relative order
In-place with O(log n) stack space

Typical performance: ~2-3x faster than merge sort/heap sort in practice due to cache efficiency.

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain quick sort algorithm, pivot selection, and complexity.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer:
Quick Sort is a comparison sort using divide-and-conquer. 

Algorithm: Choose pivot, partition array around pivot (elements < pivot on left, > pivot on right), recursively sort sub-arrays.

Pivot Selection Strategies:
- First element: Simple, but worst case O(n²) on sorted data
- Last element: Same as above
- Middle element: Better balance
- Random element: Avoids worst case with high probability
- Median-of-three: Median of first, middle, last elements

Partitioning:
- Lomuto scheme: Uses last element as pivot, simpler, moves pivot to final position
- Hoare scheme: Uses first element, two pointers moving toward each other, generally fewer swaps

Complexity:
- Best case: O(n log n) - perfectly balanced partitions at every level
- Average case: O(n log n) - regardless of initial order (with random pivot)
- Worst case: O(n²) - smallest or largest element always as pivot (avoided with random/methods)
- Space: O(log n) for recursive call stack (depth of recursion tree)
- Comparisons: ~n log n on average, n² in worst case

Applications: General-purpose sorting, large datasets, when cache efficiency matters.

Stability: Not stable. Equal elements may change relative order during partitioning.

Optimizations: Random pivot, median-of-three, three-way partitioning for duplicates, tail recursion elimination.

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain quick sort with algorithm, pivot selection, partitioning, and complexity analysis.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
Quick Sort: 

Algorithm: Uses divide-and-conquer paradigm. Select a pivot element from the array. Partition the remaining elements into two sub-arrays: those less than the pivot and those greater than the pivot. The pivot is now in its final position. Recursively apply the same process to the sub-arrays.

Pivot Selection:
- First/last: Simple but O(n²) on sorted data
- Random: Avoids worst case with high probability
- Median-of-three: Good balance, uses median of first/middle/last

Partitioning Schemes:
- Lomuto: pivot = arr[high], i = low-1, FOR j = low to high-1, if arr[j] < pivot: i++, swap arr[i], arr[j], finally swap arr[i+1], arr[high], return i+1
- Hoare: pivot = arr[low], i = low-1, j = high+1, REPEAT: i++, j-- UNTIL arr[i] >= pivot AND arr[j] <= pivot, swap arr[i], arr[j] UNTIL i >= j, return j

Complexity:
- Best case: O(n log n) - balanced partitions at every level (depth = log n, n work per level)
- Average case: O(n log n) - proven regardless of input (with good pivot)
- Worst case: O(n²) - when pivot is smallest or largest element always (depth = n, work = n+(n-1)+...+1)
- Space: O(log n) recursive call stack (not O(n) because tail recursion can be eliminated)
- Number of comparisons: ~1.39 n log n on average

Comparison with Other Sorts:
- vs Merge Sort: Both O(n log n), but quick sort is in-place (O(log n) vs O(n) space), merge sort is stable, quick sort is not stable
- vs Heap Sort: Both O(n log n), heap sort has guaranteed O(n log n), quick sort has worst O(n²) but faster average
- vs Insertion/Bubble/Selection: O(n²) vs O(n log n), quick sort much faster for large data

Practical Note: Quick sort is typically 2-3x faster than other O(n log n) sorts in practice due to cache locality. JavaScript's Array.prototype.sort() often uses a variant of quick sort (Timsort in modern engines).
